interpretation.Bottom line: This group is **calmer** (lower neuroticism) and **describes itself more favourably** (higher social desirability) than the panel. Both differences replicate on held-out people and survive all 5 one-criterion redefinitions. On values, money style, reflection, generosity and the hypothetical green choice, treat it as the population average. The earlier 'less reflective' (CRT) result was a scoring artefact and is withdrawn.
interpretation.Why this persona: It asks what age alone reveals. P3 sits at the other end of the same gradient.
interpretation.Extended profile (exploratory): Training members only (n = 194), no held-out check; six further scales re-derived from items. Higher self-concept clarity (d +0.43), agreeableness (+0.34), conscientiousness (+0.30) and extraversion (+0.23), all CIs excluding 0; openness (+0.07) and need for cognition (+0.10) unchanged. CIs: `research_frontier/persona_extension/`.
interpretation.Why it fits: *Observed:* both traits move steadily across age bands (neuroticism 3.14 → 2.28 from 18–29 to 65+; corrected social desirability 5.75 → 7.61). *Interpretation:* longitudinal studies find emotional stability, conscientiousness and agreeableness rising across adulthood (Roberts et al. 2006); self-concept clarity is higher in mid-life than in youth (Lodi-Smith & Roberts 2010). *Speculation:* ageing, cohort and self-presentation cannot be separated in cross-sectional data. Adjusting for social desirability shrinks the neuroticism gap from −0.50 to −0.31 SD, so part of the calm may be self-description.
interpretation.Say vs do: In the hypothetical $39 renewable offer, 43% chose renewable when it required switching (n = 49; population 36%) and 55% when it was the default (n = 40; 58%). These small samples did not establish a difference from the population, on training or held-out members (held out: 25 and 18); that is not evidence of equivalence.
interpretation.Where it breaks: This describes the group, not its members: a random 65+ member is more neurotic than a random 18–29-year-old 25% of the time. **Inside it:** the 40 members with income under $30,000 are no calmer than the population (neuroticism d −0.09, CI −0.40 to 0.22; other 65+ −0.52). Found by inspection.

interpretation.Bottom line: **Higher neuroticism** is the one dependable trait. It is the project's largest robust group difference and holds in all 6 redefinitions. The 'more spendthrift' prediction failed. The lower social desirability is fragile (it vanishes if the group is widened to 18–64), and the earlier CRT difference was a scoring artefact.
interpretation.Why this persona: It asks whether money matters within a life stage.
interpretation.Extended profile (exploratory): Training members only (n = 291), no held-out check; six further scales re-derived from items. Lower conscientiousness (d −0.48), extraversion (−0.47), self-concept clarity (−0.41), agreeableness (−0.26) and need for cognition (−0.22); openness unchanged (0.00). Within ages 18–49, adjusted for age band, the income gap is extraversion −0.47, conscientiousness −0.39 and self-concept clarity −0.25 (CIs exclude 0): income, not age. CIs: `research_frontier/persona_extension/`.
interpretation.Why it fits: *Observed:* within each age band, lower-income members are more neurotic (18–29: 3.36 vs 2.99; 30–49: 3.07 vs 2.69; age-adjusted +0.30 SD, CI 0.20 to 0.40). *Interpretation:* consistent with the documented link between financial strain and negative affect. *Speculation:* the direction is unknown (strain → distress, distress → lower earnings, or health driving both). Household income may misclassify students on parental income.
interpretation.Say vs do: When choosing renewable meant switching, 27% chose it on training data (n = 33; population 36%) but 47% on held-out members (n = 19). The tempting 'budget-constrained idealist' story **failed** the holdout, so no behavioural prediction is offered.
interpretation.Where it breaks: About a quarter of members are calmer than the median panel member. The neuroticism shift helps individual prediction by about a tenth. P2 contains 81 of P3's 197 training members. **Inside it:** the 98 members in full-time work are close to the population (neuroticism +0.20, CI −0.00 to 0.40), against +0.61 for the other 193. Found by inspection.

P3.name: P3_young_never_married
P3.selected_by: pre-registered rule in hypotheses.md H6 (src/personas.py select-p3, train only); top of results/p3_selection.csv

interpretation.Bottom line: Its robust trait, **higher neuroticism**, is the same age gradient P2 shows. Its eye-catching trait, **lower green values**, replicated as a group shift but is **fragile** (no reliable sex difference), and it barely improves individual prediction.
interpretation.Why this persona: It asks whether the pre-registered search for the most distinctive group (about 1,000 candidates) finds more than youth. Against other 18–29-year-olds it differs only on green values and conscientiousness (−0.33, CI −0.61 to −0.05); the rest is the young end of P1's gradient.
interpretation.Extended profile (exploratory): Training members only (n = 197), no held-out check; six further scales re-derived from items. Lower conscientiousness (d −0.61), self-concept clarity (−0.56), agreeableness (−0.37), extraversion (−0.36) and need for cognition (−0.29), all CIs excluding 0; openness −0.13. CIs: `research_frontier/persona_extension/`.
interpretation.Why it fits: *Observed:* never-married 18–29s score 3.25 on green values vs 3.84 for other 18–29s (−0.45 SD after adjusting for sex, income and education). *Interpretation:* marital status partly marks *who* is in the group (56% men vs 36% among other 18–29s; 21% students), but adjusting for sex does not remove the gap.
interpretation.Sex-composition caveat: Against the whole population the green gap is d −0.40 in men (n = 111) and −0.12 in women (n = 86), but within 18–29 the sex interaction is null (+0.18, CI −0.31 to 0.66). The gap vanishes without the marital criterion (all 18–29s: −0.11), and it is significant in only 3 of 6 redefinitions.
interpretation.Say vs do: **Insufficient evidence**: 33 members took the green experiment (17 and 16 per condition, below the 20 minimum).
interpretation.Where it breaks: P3 predicts individual green values no better than the population mean. 41% of its training members are also in P2. **Inside it:** the 58 members in full-time work match the population on conscientiousness (−0.07, CI −0.29 to 0.14), against −1.31 for the 50 unemployed. Found by inspection.
